extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improvisation teachers, directors and theatre practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and pedagogical guidance for creating, performing and directing improvised theatre (games, shows, rehearsals, teaching practices). Includes criteria for what counts as good impro work and detailed game-based training notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation as a theatrical art form (stories over mere comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: I see improvisation as a form of theatre that creates stories. Comedy is one form of story work we can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work as theatre: focus on narrative, dramatic choices and storytelling possibilities rather than treating improvisation as only gag-based comedy. Cultivate performers who 'have something they want to say, question, reveal.' Use literature, art, politics and world events to inform work so improvisation moves beyond parody and sitcom recycling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovate and take creative risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a risk and create something new rather than regurgitating the same work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design shows that challenge the audience (e.g., aiming to terrify or unsettle as well as entertain). Use diverse theatrical styles and forms, iterate in rehearsal, and be prepared to do only a few shows while developing the form. Innovation requires deliberate experiments and willingness to fail in pursuit of new ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal/process: admit stuckness, identify challenges, research and play
rubrics_metrics.description: In rehearsals, admit where you are in your work, what you feel stuck in, and what you want to be challenged with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss individual and group needs, research the target genre (read relevant literature, study multiple forms), then get on your feet: try, fail, play, laugh, pace, explore until you reach 'ah-ha' moments. A simple, iterative trial-and-error process is advocated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and be students of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation requires practitioners who are students of narrative in a variety of disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read new, form‑breaking novels, classic plays, Freud, Nietzsche, innovative theatre and television; bring varied narrative voices and structural ideas into improv work. Avoid relying only on film/TV/pop-culture sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on sketch/sitcom/pop-culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Recycling sketch comedy and sitcom limits your boundaries and creative potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variety matters, but if your work is dominated by gag impersonations and popular-culture riffs you limit storytelling and depth. Diversify sources and forms to expand possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your own stories; beware of copying teachers' content
rubrics_metrics.description: People naturally repeat what they've seen work; a 'bag of tricks' is normal but unhealthy if it's all you ever do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques that move narrative forward but avoid repeating scenes you've seen others do. Find original material and personal stories rather than mimicking gurus' content or mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose collaborators who understand your creative headspace but don't cast purely by friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemistry between players is important, but casting friends regardless of ability or attitude undermines quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast widely for talent; prioritize company chemistry and shared vision, but not at the cost of skill. Directors and companies should seek the best contributors rather than defaulting to friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and practice your weak areas by listing games you love and dislike
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out a list of games/scenes you love and another of games/scenes you dislike or avoid; disliked items reveal skill areas to challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: avoiding narrative games (Word At A Time, Typewriter, Story Story Die) signalled a weakness in taking responsibility for narrative. Tackle those avoided forms to open new levels of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek out inspiring teachers/players and form peer networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Find people who inspire you—other players, international or local teachers—and observe/work with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nurture inspiration by attending workshops, collaborating, forming discussions with other impro groups, and contacting other directors when feeling isolated. Peer networks provide feedback, bounce ideas, and reduce director burnout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create your own opportunities and cross-train in other forms
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only available show is pub‑prov, still create opportunities to explore other ideas and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get two or three people together to jam, try mask work, clowning, or other disciplines that challenge your improvisational skills. It’s up to practitioners to keep the creative fire alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set personal challenges per performance, but stay present for the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s good to have personal challenges and areas to develop, but being focused solely on your own work can make you unavailable to what’s happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use focused intentions (e.g., 'Tonight I will really listen' or 'I will take time to create platforms') to increase presence and supportiveness. Avoid being so self-focused that you miss offers and the scene’s needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create platforms (clear beginnings) to enable middles and endings
rubrics_metrics.description: If you start with a platform you set up better narratives: you have a beginning, something to make a middle, and a place to go for an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a platform scenes often start in the middle and have nowhere to go. Train to establish clean starting offers to make endings obvious and satisfy narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use post-show notes and assign a direct mentor; accept honest feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑show notes are a key way to discover what you need to work on; have someone act as a pal/mentor to give direct and honest notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train how people give and take notes in classes. Accept notes without arguing—direct feedback is more enlightening than generic self‑notes. If performers need validation in notes, reassess training approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directors as outside eyes: miss shows to improve the work; challenge performers beyond gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors should be prepared to work as an outside eye on shows, challenge performers to strive beyond gags, and remind improvisers they can’t hear audience disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directors may need to forgo performance opportunities to provide constructive outside feedback and to raise the company’s standards and storytelling focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and apply dramatic structure (tension, time, space, focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers often misunderstand that improvisation is an artificial dramatic form with structure and internal logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn elements of drama—dramatic tension, issues of time, space, focus—and apply them in practice. Theories (Johnstone, Theatresports) acknowledge structure; understanding alone is insufficient without practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance vulnerability with disciplined dramatic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulnerability alone won’t tell a story; it must be bridged with practical understanding of dramatic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open and willing to fail in performance, but also cultivate the skills to recognize what a scene needs. Too much reliance on rules without spontaneity (e.g., over‑reliance on structure) can be limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching foundation: build play scaffolding before practical aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need a creative sense of play underneath practical aesthetics; otherwise they can’t access the rigorous questions practical aesthetics asks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restructure units so that play, spontaneity and confidence are cultivated first, then teach practical aesthetics. Practical questions require a foundation of playful capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record/disseminate vs. ephemerality tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation’s ephemerality is both strength and weakness: recording enables study and wider dissemination, but capturing it can make it look like 'people mucking around.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the double‑edged nature: capture enough to build a body of knowledge and allow analysis, while preserving spontaneity where appropriate. Use dissemination (books, recordings) to advance practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise the bar: treat improv as theatre and demand platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: The mission is to raise the quality of improv work and secure platforms so it’s seen as theatre rather than relegated to rooms above pubs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize rehearsals, cast widely, come to workshops with new ideas, create company goals, collaborate between companies, attend/create festivals to share innovations, and use networking sites (e.g., yesand.com) to share discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, solicit feedback, have director watch, and iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Test new forms on audiences, solicit feedback, have an outside director watch, then work on it and perform again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterate: show, listen to feedback, rehearse with a director’s eye, and repeat performances. Embrace cycles of failure and improvement rather than striving for immediate perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept failure and avoid perfectionism; 'enjoy being bad'
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s not enough to be okay with failure—enjoying being bad can release performers to make better work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Struggling for perfection kills work. Make company goals clear, then be playful and generous on stage. Use paradox of striving in rehearsal and releasing in performance to create stronger work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Games taxonomy: Good Games, Dumb but Fun, Never Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Games are divided into: Good Games (teach/promote habits/sustain variety), Dumb but Fun (not destructive but peripheral), and Never Play (destructive/pointless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the taxonomy to choose training and performance games responsibly. Prefer Good Games for skill development, allow Dumb but Fun sparingly, and avoid Never Play games that rely on novelty or showboating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Games criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Games have something to teach you, promote good habits or sustain endless variety in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select games that develop desired skills (boldness, narrative, assumption, justification) and that can be used repeatedly without becoming stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal Expert game: keep the promise, avoid waffle, make specific details
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert scenes promise a strange expertise (e.g., dolphins playing snooker). Weak experts waffle; strong interviewers force justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay off the suggestion by inventing specific details that tie the animal and activity (how does the animal hold the cue; is the table dry?). Train experts to start answering right away and to justify absurdity. Performance use: follow a broad physical scene or when audience wants jokes; workshop use: train boldness, assumptions, jumping and justifying. Avoid inventing properties that merely solve problems in a lazy way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arms Through game guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: One person stands behind another and thrusts their arms forward; one is responsible for dialogue, the other for gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the arms character pantomiming all dialogue; allow them to make important offers. Best foregrounding: have arms character give a lecture while manipulating mime objects. Avoid versions with large tables of props or pockets full of objects as they tend to be 'stupid.' Use two or three arms characters for richness but avoid turning sideways which wrecks the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death In A Minute game guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improvisers must complete a scene in sixty seconds, during which one must kill the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners often misinterpret and build towards a long murder; daring play drops dead earlier (e.g., 10–15 seconds) forcing the survivor to justify cause and dispose of body. In performance: useful for challenge formats like Theatresports but not generally entertaining. In workshops: excellent for 'unfreezing' planners.

rubrics_metrics.name: MC role: set tone, manage voice and audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The MC has the mandate to get everyone on the same page and set the tone of the space; early MCing involved nervousness and vocal strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control engagement by calibrating tone (avoid being too dark/sarcastic without softening it). The MC can allow safe transgressive persona if balanced with warmth ('I mean that in a loving and kind way'). MCing offers structured, long-form improvisation and different creative satisfactions compared to short-form play.
